#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when excluding a dependency fixes the build but breaks runtime*
This scenario demonstrates excluding a transitive dependency from one declaration, and the silence that follows.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibB -.->|excluded| LibC[lib-c:1.0.0]
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s5-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
`lib-c` is pruned from the graph under `lib-a`, and the build carries on as if `lib-b` never needed it.

#### ! Actual
Exactly that. `lib-c` disappears from the classpath with no warning. If `lib-b` loads a `lib-c` class at runtime, the first sign is `NoClassDefFoundError`.

#### ! Why
`.exclude(group, artifact)` tells Coursier to drop the named artifact wherever it appears beneath that declaration, at any depth. The resolver does not know whether `lib-b` can function without `lib-c`; it only knows you asked. Exclusions are path-scoped: if a second direct dependency also brings `lib-c`, that path is untouched and `lib-c` comes back (see SB18 for the build-wide form).

#### ! Fix
*   **Swap an implementation:** the most common legitimate use is replacing a logging backend, excluding `log4j` and adding Logback, or excluding a vulnerable transitive and declaring a patched version directly.
*   **Prefer an override to an exclusion** when the problem is the *version* of `lib-c`, not its presence: `dependencyOverrides` (SB6) keeps the dependency and changes the version.
*   **Build-wide ban:** when `lib-c` must never appear through any path, use `excludeDependencies += ExclusionRule("com.demo", "lib-c")` (SB18) rather than repeating `.exclude` on every declaration.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Replacing an implementation (`log4j` with `logback`) and adding the replacement explicitly.
* MEDIUM Excluding a transitive you believe is unused, without a test that exercises the code path that might need it.
* HIGH Excluding to "fix" a conflict without verifying compatibility; the build goes green and the runtime throws `NoClassDefFoundError`.

#### ! Control
Comment every exclusion with the reason and, where one exists, the upstream issue. Re-check exclusions whenever the excluded library's consumer is upgraded; the new version may need what you removed.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** `lib-b` with no `lib-c` child beneath it, and no marker that anything was removed.

**Conclusion:** The exclusion silently prunes `lib-c` from this path.

#### ! Scales
In large Scala projects, exclusions accumulate as different library ecosystems bring in conflicting versions of common dependencies, particularly around Scala binary-version suffixes and cross-builds. Exclusion management becomes one of the primary maintenance burdens of an sbt build, and each exclusion is a silent assumption that nothing on that path needs the artifact.

#### ! Takeaway
`.exclude` removes an artifact from one path, silently. Use it to swap implementations, not to make conflicts disappear.

#### ! Wild

A recurring issue in Scala ecosystems occurs when libraries depend on different [Scala binary versions](https://docs.scala-lang.org/overviews/core/binary-compatibility-of-scala-releases.html) (for example 2.12 vs 2.13). Because Scala encodes the binary version into artifact names (`library_2.12` vs `library_2.13`), mixing versions causes `NoSuchMethodError` or `ClassNotFoundException` at runtime. Teams resolve this by excluding the unwanted variant and adding a direct dependency on the aligned version. The [sbt cross-building documentation](https://www.scala-sbt.org/1.x/docs/Cross-Build.html) covers the underlying mechanism.
